etymology: Hebrew Moladah, perhaps “birth” or “generation,” a town of the Negeb in the south of Judah.
biblical_def: Moladah was a town in the uttermost south of Judah, named among the cities “toward the coast of Edom southward” in the great catalogue of Judah’s inheritance (Jos 15:21, 26). When the lot of Simeon fell within the inheritance of the children of Judah, because the portion of Judah was too large for them, Moladah was reckoned among the cities given to Simeon (Jos 19:1–2). Thus it belonged to the dry southland, the Negeb, that parched and thirsty frontier where Israel learned to depend upon the LORD for wells and rain. The town does not vanish from the record after the conquest, for after the captivity the children of Judah returning from Babylon dwelt again at Moladah and the villages thereof (Neh 11:26). So the same town settled at the entrance into the land was re-inhabited by the remnant the LORD brought home, a quiet testimony that He does not forget the least-known places of His people’s heritage. Moladah, whose name may speak of birth and generation, stands as a witness that the God who gave the land also keeps it, settling Simeon safely within Judah and bringing His people back to their old borders after the long affliction of exile.

biblical_def: Hazar-shual, “the village of the jackal” or “court of the fox,” was a town in the southland of Judah, named in the catalogue of the cities given to that tribe in the uttermost south (Jos 15:28). Like the towns about it, it fell within the inheritance of Simeon, whose lot the LORD set in the midst of Judah because Judah’s portion was more than they needed (Jos 19:1, 3). Its very name, drawn from the wild creatures that haunt the dry and desolate places, speaks of the harshness of the Negeb, the thirsty frontier where the wells were few and the wilderness pressed close upon the settlements of God’s people. Such a place was a school of dependence, where Israel could not trust in abundance but must look to the LORD for water and life. Hazar-shual too was remembered after the captivity, for the children of Judah dwelt there again among the towns re-inhabited by the returning remnant (Neh 11:27). The town of the jackal, set on the edge of the waste, stands as a witness that the LORD plants His people even in hard and barren places, and keeps them there by His provision; the dry south was a place of testing, but the God of the wells was faithful in it.

etymology: Hebrew Madmannah, perhaps “dunghill” or “place of dung,” a town in the south of Judah.
biblical_def: Madmannah was a town in the southland of Judah, named in the catalogue of the cities given to that tribe in the uttermost south, toward the border of Edom (Jos 15:31). It lay among the towns of the dry Negeb, that thirsty frontier where the LORD planted His people and proved them by the scarcity of the land. In the genealogies of Judah in the Chronicles the name appears as a man, for Shaaph the son of Caleb’s concubine Maachah is called the father of Madmannah (1Ch 2:49), after the Hebrew manner whereby the founder or chief of a town is named its father. Thus the town was reckoned to the house of Caleb, that faithful man who wholly followed the LORD and received his inheritance in the south. Madmannah’s name, lowly in its meaning, sits among the obscure villages of the southland that the world would never have remembered, save that the LORD wrote them into His word. The town stands as a witness that God numbers and keeps even the meanest places of His people’s heritage; the dry south was a place of testing, but no village in it was beneath the notice of the God who gave the whole land by lot to the tribes of His covenant.

Its name, drawn from the lionesses that once haunted the wild and desolate country of the Negeb, speaks of the harshness of that southern frontier, where the beasts of the field pressed close upon the settlements of God’s people. To dwell in such a land was to live in dependence upon the LORD, who keeps His people in the midst of danger and gives them rest among the lions’ dens. Lebaoth is one of the obscure towns of the south that left no further mark in the sacred history, yet it was written into the word of God among the inheritance of Simeon. etymology: Hebrew Qabts’el, “God gathers” or “whom God gathers,” the southernmost town of Judah.
biblical_def: Kabzeel, “God gathers,” was the southernmost of all the towns of Judah, named first in the catalogue of the uttermost cities of the tribe toward the coast of Edom (Jos 15:21). It stood at the very edge of the inheritance, on the dry frontier of the Negeb, where the land of promise gave way to the wilderness and the borders of Edom. Yet this obscure border town was honoured above its fellows as the birthplace of a mighty man: Benaiah the son of Jehoiada, “the son of a valiant man, of Kabzeel, who had done many acts” (2Sa 23:20; 1Ch 11:22). Benaiah slew two lionlike men of Moab, went down and slew a lion in the midst of a pit in time of snow, and struck down a great Egyptian with the Egyptian’s own spear; he was set by David over his guard and afterward made captain of the host under Solomon. Thus from the least and farthest town of Judah the LORD raised up one of the foremost of the mighty men. Kabzeel stands as a witness that God gathers His servants from the obscure frontiers of His people, and that the place of one’s birth is no measure of the place to which the LORD may call him; the town whose name confesses that God gathers brought forth a valiant man gathered to the service of the king.
